headline: Slow a kid's growth down
body: It's called catch-up growth and it shouldn't be possible if height ran on a clock.
punch: The fact it happens tells you what height actually runs on.

headline: If growth were a timer
body: Illness, malnutrition, glucocorticoids. Anything that suppresses growth for months should cost you those months permanently. It doesn't.
punch: Take the brake off and growth rate goes above normal for age.

headline: Because suppressing growth
body: Growth plates hold a finite number of cell divisions. Slow the division rate down and you slow how fast that reserve depletes.
punch: You didn't lose time. You just spent the account slower.

headline: This has been tested
body: It's not specific to one hormone. Hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid excess and other unrelated growth inhibitors all delay growth plate senescence the same way.
punch: Senescence tracks how much you've divided, not your age.

headline: It even works
body: Infuse a growth inhibitor into one rabbit tibia and only that plate slows down. Then only that plate overshoots afterwards. The other leg does nothing.
punch: Which rules out any systemic or brain based explanation.

headline: But there is a limit
body: Estrogen does two separate things. It suppresses growth rate, which is fully reversible. And it structurally depletes the progenitor pool, which isn't. That was still measurable five weeks after treatment stopped.
punch: One of those you get back. The other you don't.

headline: Which is the real split
body: Slowed growth can be recovered. Spent cells can't. Two things can look identical on a growth chart and leave you somewhere completely different.
punch: The chart won't tell you which one happened.

headline: And catch-up isn't unlimited
body: It's well documented after temporary suppression. Whether it fully restores predicted adult height depends on how long, how severe and when. Often it doesn't.
punch: Partial recovery is the normal outcome, not full.
